title: Senate Bean Soup (Fast, Canned Beans)
source: NYT Cooking - Sarah DiGregorio (the recipe's own faster-version tip)
ingredients: 1 red or yellow onion, finely chopped
3 medium carrots, peeled and sliced 1/2 to 1 inch thick
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, Diamond Crystal (half the original Tbsp - see notes)
8 cups chicken broth (in place of the water)
4 (15-oz) cans navy beans, drained and rinsed
About 1 lb chopped ham (in place of the ham hocks)
1 medium russet potato, peeled and quartered
OPTIONAL: 8 oz kale, stems removed and chopped
steps: Melt the butter in a large soup pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, 5-6 min until softened.
Add the garlic and carrots and cook, stirring, about 2 min until the garlic is fragrant and softened.
Add the salt, smoked paprika, thyme and several generous grinds of black pepper. Stir to combine.
Add the broth, drained beans, chopped ham and potato. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer, cover, and simmer 20-30 min - until the potato is tender and the soup has come together.
Add the kale, if using, in the last 5 min.
Mash the potato pieces against the side of the pot with a fork. Stir vigorously to break down some of the beans too - that is what thickens it.
Stir in the cider vinegar. Taste and add salt and pepper as needed.
notes: This is the recipe's own TIP for a faster version, not a workaround: four 15-oz cans of navy beans for the dried, chopped ham for the ham hocks, chicken broth for the water, salt cut in half, and a 20-30 min simmer instead of the hour-plus. SALT: the original calls for 1 Tbsp kosher salt (Diamond Crystal) with plain water and unsalted dried beans; the tip says halve it, so 1 1/2 tsp. Even that can run high once you factor in salted broth, canned beans and ham - if you are using regular (not low-sodium) broth, start at 1 tsp and season at the end. If you use Morton kosher or table salt, cut it further; Diamond Crystal is much less salty by volume. RINSE THE BEANS - the canning liquid is starchy and salty. THICKENING: canned beans do not release starch the way a long simmer does, so the potato mash and crushing some of the beans matters more here than in the original. Still thin? Mash more beans or simmer a few minutes uncovered. The vinegar at the end is not optional - it is what keeps it from tasting flat.
